newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin returns to Moscow fray after "good rest".
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin returns to Moscow fray after "good rest".

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin plunges back into a busy work schedule on Wednesday after a month-long summer vacation, but will find many problems including a nasty political row have been brewing during his absence.

Yeltsin, who left Moscow on July 6, looked refreshed and cheerful on Tuesday as he said goodbye to officials and well-wishers in the central region of Samara where he spent the second part of his vacation.
"I have had a very good rest," he told reporters before boarding the plane with his wife Naina.
The 66-year-old president has staged a strong recovery from heart surgery last November and, a year into his second term of office, appears to have a firmer grip on power than ever.

One of the first issues awaiting his attention back in the Kremlin is the controversial sale of a controlling stake in Russian mining giant Norilsk Nickel against the wishes of Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and other senior officials.

The tender was won on Tuesday by a partner of commercial bank Uneximbank, which is already under fire from large sections of the mass media for winning a quarter stake in Russia's telecommunications company Svyazinvest last week.
The Svyazinvest sale pitted several powerful banking and media tycoons against Yeltsin's new liberal team led by First Deputy Prime Ministers Boris Nemtsov and Anatoly Chubais.
Chernomyrdin and top privatisation official Alfred Kokh had urged a delay in the sale of Norilsk Nickel for an unspecified period. Critics of the tender say its terms were unfair.
"It is not yet clear what will be the reaction of Chernomyrdin to the fact that his order was ignored," the daily Moskovsky Komsomolyets said in its Wednesday edition.
The veteran prime minister has seen his political influence ebb as Chubais and Nemtsov have begun setting the pace for reforms, but he may try to resist Uneximbank's latest purchases.

"The fact that the (Norilsk Nickel) tender went ahead does not prevent the state in the form of the State Prosecutor's office from contesting its outcome in court," Interfax news agency quoted Sergei Molozhavy, deputy president of the State Property Fund, as saying on Tuesday.
The Norilsk and Svyazinvest sales are part of a fresh round of big state sell-offs in Russia expected to raise a total $4-5 billion for state coffers in 1997 alone.

Last week Nemtsov and Chubais, struggling to balance the state budget with improved tax collection and big spending cuts, praised the Svyazinvest sale, saying the money would help pay off debts to Russia's military, doctors and teachers.
Millions of state workers and soldiers have gone many months without pay due to a big shortfall in tax revenue. Yeltsin has made their plight his top political priority.
Interfax said Yeltsin would hold talks on Wednesday with the chief of Russia's powerful gas monopoly, Rem Vyakhirev, on problems facing the gas industry, but gave no details.

Yeltsin was also due to attend the consecration of a new chapel in the heart of Moscow with Patriarch Alexiy, head of the Russian Orthodox Church. He was expected to try to repair ties damaged by a recent spat over a controversial law on religion.
The church, which usually keeps clear of politics, gave strong backing to the bill, which would have imposed tough curbs on so-called "non-traditional" religious groups in Russia.

Yeltsin vetoed the bill while on holiday, saying it contravened Russia's post-Soviet constitution guaranteeing equality to all creeds. But he has also signalled that he wants to improve his usually good relations with the church.
Later this week Yeltsin will meet Turkmenistan President Saparmurat Niyazov for talks on the tricky issue of the Caspian Sea and its natural resources, including oil.

Yeltsin may also invite Chechen leader Aslan Maskhadov to Moscow in early August to try to break a deadlock over a political treaty mapping out future relations between Russia and its breakaway Caucasus region, Itar-Tass news agency said.
